title: Penetrant Testing Stainless Steel | Low-Halogen PT (US)
description: Dye penetrant testing of stainless, duplex and nickel alloys with certified low-halogen, low-sulfur materials, mobilized across the US. Request a PT quote.
h1: Penetrant Testing of Stainless Steel and Nickel Alloys: Low-Halogen PT
html:
Penetrant testing of stainless steel and nickel alloys needs materials with controlled sulfur and halogen content, a clean surface, and full removal of residues afterward. Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians across the United States to examine austenitic and duplex stainless, nickel alloys and titanium in chemical, LNG, power and processing plants, using low-halogen penetrants and documented lot certification. Request a PT inspection quote with your alloy list.

Why these alloys need their own penetrant procedure

Penetrant finds only flaws that are surface-breaking, so the metal's own surface chemistry is the whole story. Carbon steel shrugs off most of what penetrant chemistry leaves behind. Stainless steel, nickel alloys and titanium do not. These metals rely on a thin passive film, and sulfur, chlorine and fluorine left in contact with a hot or stressed surface can damage that film. The risks named in practice are pitting, intergranular attack on nickel-base alloys from sulfur, and stress corrosion cracking of austenitic stainless from chlorides when the part runs warm under tensile stress, which describes most weld heat-affected zones. For titanium, chlorine and fluorine are the main concern.

This is the reason ASME Section V Article 6 sets contaminant limits for penetrant materials used on these alloys and requires that each batch be certified. Our procedures follow that article and ASTM E165, and the batch certificates go to site with the crew and into the report.

Alloys we examine

  • Austenitic stainless (304, 304L, 316, 316L, 321, 347). Non-magnetic, so MT is not possible. Penetrant is the surface method for welds, castings and machined parts.
  • Duplex and super-duplex. Two-phase structure with higher strength and good chloride resistance. Penetrant is the standard surface method and is preferred over magnetic particle because the ferrite content gives uneven magnetic response.
  • Nickel alloys (Alloy 600, 625, 825, C-276 and similar). Sulfur is the controlled contaminant. Overlay and dissimilar-metal welds are examined at fusion boundaries.
  • Titanium. Chlorine and fluorine limits apply, and cleaning chemistry must be compatible.
  • 9 percent nickel and other cryogenic steels. Magnetic, but residual magnetism and stainless weld metal often lead specifications toward penetrant.

Contaminant control in practice

Article 6 states the contaminant limits and how they are verified. In practice that means four things on every stainless or nickel job:

  1. The penetrant, remover and developer are bought as a matched, labeled set, with the manufacturer's certification for sulfur and halogen content for the lot we are using.
  2. Cleaning solvents are from the same low-halogen family. Chlorinated solvents that were once common are not used.
  3. Rags, brushes and wipes are new or dedicated to this alloy. Brushes used on carbon steel are never used on stainless, because embedded iron causes rust spots.
  4. Spray cans are labeled so aerosol and bulk products are not mixed within a job, and the cleaner is applied to a wipe, not sprayed across the surface.

We list product names and lot numbers in the report, so your quality department can trace what touched the equipment.

Chloride stress corrosion cracking and what PT can show

Austenitic stainless that has been in chloride-bearing service, such as coastal plants, cooling water, steam condensate, or insulation that stays wet, can develop branched, transgranular cracks that are tight and often hard to see. Penetrant is good at finding them on the surface if the surface is clean, the cracks are not smeared, and the dwell is long enough. A skilled technician reads branching, mud-crack patterns and indications that grow slowly as typical. Penetrant does not tell you how deep the cracks go; that needs another method and your engineer's assessment. We do not determine fitness for service.

Surface condition and finishing sequence

The order of operations matters. Welds should be cleaned, with heat tint removed where the specification requires, before penetrant testing, so oxide does not mask flaws. Pickling or passivation to ASTM A967 or A380 practice is normally done after the examination and after any repairs, so the passive film is not removed and re-damaged. Grinding stainless with abrasive wheels closes tight cracks, which is why prepared surfaces are checked and light etching may be needed. If your fabrication plan puts passivation before PT, tell us so the cleaning step can be defined.

Material-specific notes by industry

In hygienic plants the main objects are tanks, jackets and process lines, and the cleaning rules are set by the plant; the food and pharma penetrant page covers those. In chemical plants the service fluid decides which welds get the most scrutiny, and caustic or chloride duty is common. On LNG and cryogenic equipment, stainless and 9 percent nickel dominate and cleanliness for low-temperature service is critical. In petrochemical units overlay, clad pipe and exchanger tubesheets are typical, and in power plants stainless superheater and feedwater components, valve bodies and turbine-related parts are examined at outages.

For oxygen service and some high-purity systems, hydrocarbon residue is itself a hazard, because oil-based penetrant can remain in crevices. Equipment on oxygen service is normally cleaned to a specification such as the Compressed Gas Association's oxygen cleaning practice after any penetrant work, and the work is planned with the owner's cleaning specialist.

Technique details that matter on stainless

  • Temperature. The Article 6 standard range is 40 to 125 °F (5 to 52 °C). Stainless held at a cold plant or on a warm jacket falls outside, and the procedure is qualified at the actual temperature or the surface is brought into range.
  • Dwell. Tight stress corrosion cracks and crater cracks need longer dwell than pores. Dwell time is taken from the procedure and verified on a comparator block when needed.
  • Sensitivity. Visible solvent-removable dye is the field default; fluorescent systems, classed by sensitivity level, are used where the specification asks for higher sensitivity and a darkened area is possible.
  • Surface roughness. Polished and electropolished faces give a clean background but very fine flaws need magnification and good light.
  • Background. Ground and brushed finishes can retain penetrant; the remover step is adapted so the surface is not over-removed.

Flaws typical of stainless and nickel welds

Austenitic welds solidify with a tendency toward hot cracking, particularly in fully austenitic compositions and where a weld is restrained, so crater cracks and centerline cracks are the first things a technician looks for. Heat-affected zones in nickel alloys can show liquation cracks. Lack of fusion between passes is common when a stainless weld is cleaned poorly between layers. Porosity appears when shielding or back purge is lost. Clad and overlay welds can disbond or crack at the fusion line with the base metal, and tubesheet-to-tube welds in exchangers show cracks that start at the crevice. In each case penetrant gives location and length at the surface, which feeds your repair decision.

Cast and wrought forms

Stainless castings such as CF8M valve bodies and pump casings have rough, porous skins that hold penetrant in the surface texture, so water-washable or carefully removed systems are used and the background is judged with the casting standard in mind. Our penetrant testing of castings page covers that case. Forgings, bar stock and machined parts are cleaner and give crisp indications; laps and seams from forging show up as straight lines along the grain.

Planning realities for alloy work

Technicians are mobilized to your site for an agreed scope, and the chemistry is controlled from the first day. We bring dedicated, labeled consumables rather than buying locally, so the lot certificates match what is used. Plants may require approval of each product before it enters the area, and cleanliness specifications may call for witness of the final wipe. Outdoor and cold-weather work is limited by the standard temperature range, and indoor staging under a tent or in a heated shop is often practical. Hot-work, confined space and lockout permits are arranged ahead of time through your site contact.

Inspection planning for outages

Stainless and nickel-alloy examinations are often concentrated in turnarounds and outages, when exchangers, vessels and piping are open. We recommend sending the weld list and alloy map early, so lot certificates, matching consumables and cleaning steps are ready before the crew mobilizes. Where parts are returned from service, fouling and process residue have to be removed before penetrant can enter flaws, and the cleaning method needs to be compatible with the alloy. The turnaround and shutdown inspection page explains how our crews fit into those windows.

What the report contains

The report names the part or weld and its drawing reference, alloy and heat number where available, the procedure and revision, the penetrant system with manufacturer, product names and lot numbers, the sulfur and halogen certification references, temperatures, dwell and developer times, the technician and level, the indications with sketches and sizes, and accept or reject against the named code. Post-cleaning steps and any plant cleaning verification references are attached. An ASNT Level III reviews it. Remaining life, material selection and release to service stay with your engineer.

What to send for a quote

  • Alloy grades and product forms: weld, plate, casting, forging, tube.
  • Drawings or weld maps and the joints to be examined.
  • Governing code, edition and acceptance criteria, plus any cleanliness specification.
  • Service fluid, temperature, and whether the equipment is new or in service.
  • Rules on chemicals and residues for the area.
  • Access, permits and the site address.

Where we work in the United States

  • Indianapolis for pharmaceutical and food stainless in Indiana.
  • Philadelphia for stainless process piping in drug and specialty chemical plants.
  • Newark for stainless and nickel-alloy piping in New Jersey chemical and pharmaceutical plants.
  • Boston for high-purity skids and cleanroom piping in Massachusetts.
  • Houston for duplex and nickel-alloy equipment along the Ship Channel.
  • Lake Charles for chemical and LNG-export-related stainless in southwest Louisiana.
  • Chicago for stainless fabrication and process plants.
  • Memphis for food, chemical and fabrication plants in the mid-South.

Train your own technicians

Teams that run their own penetrant program can use PT Level 1 and PT Level 2 training. The training explains contaminant control in the context of SNT-TC-1A, where your employer certifies its technicians.

What we do not do here

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, does not run specialist techniques covered elsewhere, and does not decide material selection, passivation or fitness for service. The penetrant testing overview covers the method more broadly.

faq.q: Why does stainless steel need low-halogen penetrant?
faq.a: Chlorine and fluorine left on austenitic stainless or titanium can pit the passive film and, with heat and tensile stress, start stress corrosion cracking. ASME Section V Article 6 therefore limits halogen and sulfur content in penetrant materials used on these alloys and requires batch certification.

faq.q: What is the concern with sulfur on nickel alloys?
faq.a: Sulfur can attack nickel-base alloys at elevated temperature and cause embrittlement or intergranular damage. Article 6 limits sulfur in penetrant materials for nickel-base alloys, and we obtain the manufacturer's certification for each lot before using it.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle testing be used on duplex stainless?
faq.a: Duplex contains ferrite and responds to a magnet, but the response is uneven and not suited to a reliable particle indication, so penetrant is the standard surface method. Fully austenitic grades are not magnetic at all, which rules out magnetic particle testing.

faq.q: Does penetrant testing find chloride stress corrosion cracks?
faq.a: Yes, when the cracks are open to a clean surface and the dwell is long enough. It shows their surface pattern and length but not their depth. Depth and fitness for service are matters for your engineer, using other data.

faq.q: Should penetrant testing be done before or after passivation?
faq.a: It is normally done after weld cleaning and any repairs but before final pickling or passivation, so the passive film is formed on a finished surface. If your fabrication plan differs, tell us and the cleaning steps are written to suit it.

faq.q: What happens to penetrant residue in crevices?
faq.a: Residue left in crevices can trap chlorides or oil. The procedure includes remover and wipe steps, and for hygienic or oxygen service the plant's own cleaning verification follows. We record the products and methods used so the cleaning plan can take over.

faq.q: How is PT on stainless different from PT on carbon steel?
faq.a: The technique is the same, but the materials are certified low in sulfur and halogens, solvents are chosen with the alloy in mind, tools are dedicated to stainless to avoid iron contamination, and post-cleaning is more rigorous. Carbon steel can often be tested magnetically instead.

faq.q: Can you test titanium and nickel-alloy welds?
faq.a: Yes. Titanium needs chlorine and fluorine controlled, and nickel alloys need sulfur controlled. We select materials certified for those alloys, write the procedure, and examine welds, overlays and machined parts under the code you name.

faq.q: What do you need to quote penetrant testing on alloys?
faq.a: Send the alloy grades, product forms, drawings or weld maps, governing code and acceptance criteria, service conditions, cleanliness requirements, chemical restrictions, access details and the site address. We then specify the materials, procedure and report before mobilizing.
